::: {.oneline}
Every spectroscopy disturbs a sample and records what comes back, so that as
long as the disturbance is weak, every spectroscopy measures the same kind of
object.
:::

## Short answer

If we strip any spectroscopy down, the same three steps remain: we bring in
something that couples to the sample, we let the sample react, and we detect the
reaction. Light in and light out, electrons in and electrons out, a magnetic
field switched on and a magnetization measured.

Since good measurements are deliberately gentle (we do not want the probe to
change what we are measuring) the reaction is proportional to the disturbance.
That proportionality is a response function, and it belongs to the sample. The
apparatus only decides *which* response function, that is, which property of the
sample is pushed, which one is watched, and how much energy and momentum are
handed over.

This is why an absorption spectrum, an electron energy-loss spectrum and a
resonant scattering spectrum can be discussed in the same breath. They probe the
same class of excitations with different couplings and different accessible
momentum, which is also why they emphasize different features of one and the
same system.

It also explains something that would otherwise look like a coincidence. The
function describing how a system absorbs energy also describes how it fluctuates
on its own, in equilibrium, with nothing pushing it at all. Absorbing and
fluctuating are indeed two views of the same internal dynamics.

## Why it works this way

The alternative would be for each instrument to measure its own private
quantity, with no way of comparing them. Linear response is thus what makes
spectroscopy a science rather than a catalogue of machine readings, though only
within its domain of validity. If we push hard enough, a fixed response function
stops being a useful notion, which is precisely the regime in which nonlinear
and pump–probe spectroscopy operate.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## The algebra: same kernel, different couplings

| Technique | Perturbation | Observable |
|---|---|---|
| Optical absorption | $\mathbf E(t)$ | polarization $\hat{\mathbf P}$ |
| EELS | Coulomb field of the beam | density $\hat n_{\mathbf q}$ |
| Photoemission | photon field | removal of one electron |
| Magnetic susceptibility | $\mathbf B(t)$ | magnetization $\hat{\mathbf M}$ |

Each row is the same
[Kubo expression](../what-is-a-response-function/index.qmd) with a different
operator pair.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## The algebra: fluctuation–dissipation

In equilibrium at temperature $T$, the dissipative part of the response and the
spontaneous fluctuations of the same quantity are related by

$$
S(\omega) = \frac{2\hbar}{1 - e^{-\hbar\omega/k_B T}}\,
\operatorname{Im}\chi(\omega) ,
$$ {#eq-fluctuation-dissipation}

which is why a measurement of noise and a measurement of absorption return the
same physics. Out of equilibrium this relation fails, and the two must be
computed separately.
:::

## Common confusions

- **"A different technique measures a different thing."** It often measures the
  same excitations through a different coupling, which changes what is visible
  and not what exists.
- **"Nonlinear spectroscopy measures a nonlinear response function."** It
  measures a hierarchy of them, of which the linear one remains the leading
  term.
